passage: "Hafsa, the radio says the cyclone might reach the coast tonight. Help me fill the water buckets." "Noor Appi, they say that every year." Hafsa didn't look up from her phone. "Last time it was just rain." "This time the fishermen didn't go out. Ammi's already packed the documents." "Ammi packs the documents if a cloud looks at her." Hafsa scrolled past a video of waves. "Nothing ever happens on our street." "Then fill the buckets for nothing. Ten minutes." "After this video." Outside the window, the coconut palms were bending lower than Hafsa had ever seen. She glanced up once, then back at the screen. "Hafsa." "I heard you! It's fine. It's always fine." Noor dragged the buckets alone. The wind rattled the tin roof of the shed, and Hafsa turned the volume up.

qa.q: What had Ammi already done?
qa.a: Ammi had already packed the documents.

qa.q: Why does Hafsa feel so sure the cyclone won't matter?
qa.a: Past warnings ended in "just rain" and nothing ever happens on her street, so the ordinary past makes her feel safe tonight too.

qa.q: Which moment could have been Hafsa's turning point, and what could she have done then?
qa.a: When she saw the palms bending lower than ever. She could have put the phone down and helped fill the buckets, because the signs were different this time.

qa.q: What is it like for Noor to drag the buckets alone?
qa.a: Noor is worried and doing the work while Hafsa brushes off every warning, which could leave Noor frustrated as well as anxious.

grounding: A teenage girl waves off a cyclone warning because past warnings came to nothing, and keeps scrolling as the wind rises.

passage: I'm Mridul, and I still think about that August evening. The district alert came as a text: the river was rising, and low areas should move valuables up and be ready to leave. Sumit messaged, "We're shifting to my uncle's place, you?" I sent back a laughing face. Our lane had never flooded in my whole life. I lay on the bed scrolling cricket clips while Baba stacked the rice sacks on the table, and I honestly felt calm, as if the alert was meant for some other town. At two in the morning the water came under the door. We carried the books and the gas cylinder upstairs in the dark, Baba shouting, my little sister crying. Nobody got hurt. But my schoolbag, left on the floor, was ruined. Now when an alert comes, I don't check my memory first. I check the alert.

qa.q: What did Sumit's message say?
qa.a: "We're shifting to my uncle's place, you?"

qa.q: Why did Mridul feel calm while Baba stacked the rice sacks?
qa.a: Mridul's lane had never flooded, so the alert felt meant for some other town rather than for their own home.

qa.q: What does Mridul now do differently when an alert comes, and why is that wiser?
qa.a: Mridul checks the alert instead of trusting memories of past years, because a lane that never flooded can still flood.

qa.q: How might Sumit have taken Mridul's laughing reply?
qa.a: Sumit, whose family was already leaving, may have felt uneasy or brushed off, seeing a friend treat a real warning as a joke.

grounding: A teenager looks back on scrolling through a flood alert because the lane had never flooded before.

passage: Note from Shalini, hostel warden, Friday evening. The cyclone alert came at 4 pm and we moved the girls to the ground-floor hall with torches and water. Kavitha, Class 9, stayed on her bed in Room 12, scrolling her phone. When I went up, she said, "Ma'am, this happens every monsoon. Nothing ever comes." She wasn't being rude; she looked genuinely relaxed, even amused at the fuss. The windows were already rattling. I sat on the next bed and said, "You may be right. But the alert isn't about last year. It's about tonight." She rolled her eyes, but she came down. At 9 pm a branch smashed the window of Room 12. Kavitha went very quiet when she saw the glass. Tomorrow I'll talk with her, not to scold, just to hear what she thinks now.

qa.q: What happened at 9 pm?
qa.a: A branch smashed the window of Room 12.

qa.q: What does Kavitha going very quiet at the sight of the glass suggest?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably shaken, realising that the danger she had shrugged off was real and had reached the very room where she had been lying. 😰

qa.q: What made Shalini's approach work in Room 12?
qa.a: Shalini did not argue or shame Kavitha. By granting that Kavitha might be right but pointing out the alert was about tonight, Shalini got her to come down.

qa.q: How might the other girls in the hall have seen Kavitha staying upstairs?
qa.a: They might have worried about her, or wondered whether they were overreacting, since one relaxed classmate can make a warning seem less serious.

grounding: A warden records how a teenage girl dismissed a cyclone alert as nothing new and kept scrolling until persuaded to move.

passage:
Thursday night

Red alert for Mumbai, again. Extremely heavy rain, stay indoors, blah blah. Mummy read it out like it was the end of the world. Every July they send this and every July we're fine. We're on the fourth floor. Our lane has never flooded more than ankle-deep.
So I'm annoyed because Zubin's birthday thing at the café is tomorrow and Papa says NO. I told him the alerts are for low-lying areas, not us. He said, "Low-lying areas are where you'll be travelling." Okay, whatever.
It's pouring right now. Like, loud. The TV says the local trains are slowing. I'm lying here scrolling reels and I honestly feel fine. Nothing ever actually happens to us.
Ritu

qa.q: What floor does Ritu's family live on?
qa.a: They live on the fourth floor.

qa.q: Why does Ritu feel so calm while the rain pours?
qa.a: Because every July alert so far has passed without trouble, Ritu assumes this one will too and feels safe.

qa.q: What might Ritu notice in Papa's reply that could change Ritu's thinking?
qa.a: Papa points out that the risk is on the route, not just at home; Ritu could see that a safe flat doesn't make the whole city safe.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading the alert while Ritu scrolls?
qa.a: Papa probably feels worried and a bit frustrated that Ritu is treating a real warning as routine.

grounding: A teen shrugs off a heavy-rain flood alert because nothing bad has happened before and keeps scrolling.
